explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Ruth 1:1 says the man from Bethlehem in Judah went to reside in the land of Moab with his wife and two sons. That move sets the whole story in motion. One family decision, and now here comes a whole road full of tears.
Not this time, friend. Ruth 1:1 says the family went to live in the land of Moab, not Egypt. Egypt shows up in plenty of Bible stories, but not in this opening scene. Here the road leads to Moab.

Close swing, but not this one. Ruth 1:1 says they left Bethlehem and went to reside in the land of Moab. Edom is another place in Scripture, but it is not where Naomi's family settles in this passage. Moab is the name to keep in the cookie box.

Yes indeed. Ruth 1:4 says Naomi's sons took Moabite women as their wives, one named Orpah and the other named Ruth. That is our first mention of Ruth in the book. Quiet entrance now, but do not blink on this woman.

That name belongs somewhere else in Scripture, but not here. Ruth 1:4 says the two Moabite women were Orpah and Ruth. Rachel is not one of Naomi's daughters-in-law in this passage. Ruth is the name the text gives.
Not Dinah, friend. Ruth 1:4 names the women as Orpah and Ruth. The writer keeps it simple and clear right there in the verse. Ruth is the other daughter-in-law.

That is right, and it is heavy. Ruth 1:5 says both Mahlon and Chilion died, and Naomi was left without her two sons and without her husband. The verse wants you to feel how alone she is now. The story begins in famine, and then the losses keep landing.

explanations.answer: Her house in Moab burns down
explanations.explanation: The passage does not say that. Ruth 1:5 says both of Naomi's sons died after they had lived in Moab about ten years. The loss here is not her house but her family. That is why the verse ends by saying she was left without her husband and her two sons.

explanations.answer: She falls sick and loses her sight
explanations.explanation: That is not what happens in the text. Ruth 1:5 says both Mahlon and Chilion died. The verse puts all the weight on Naomi being left without her husband and without her two sons. It is a lonely sentence, and the writer means it to be.

Perfect bake! Ruth 1:6 says Naomi heard in Moab that the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food. That news is what gets her ready to leave Moab. The famine opened the story, and now food starts turning people back toward Bethlehem.

Not here, baker. Ruth 1:6 says Naomi heard that the LORD had provided His people with food. The verse is about relief from famine, not the arrival of a king. Food is the thing that changes the road ahead.

That would be a different kind of news, but not this news. Ruth 1:6 says the LORD attended to His people by providing them with food. The problem in this chapter began with famine in Ruth 1:1, so food is the answer named here. The text keeps its eye on survival.

explanations.answer: Go back to their mothers' homes
explanations.explanation: Yes, that is exactly what Naomi says. In Ruth 1:8, she tells her two daughters-in-law, "Go back, each of you to your mother's home." She also asks the LORD to show them loving devotion. Naomi is trying to send them toward what she thinks is rest.

explanations.answer: Walk faster to beat the dark
explanations.explanation: Naomi never says that here. Ruth 1:8 says she tells Orpah and Ruth to go back, each of them to her mother's home. Her words are not about speed on the road but about sending them home. This is a goodbye speech, not a travel pep talk.

explanations.answer: Stay close to her the whole way
explanations.explanation: That is the opposite of what Naomi says in this moment. Ruth 1:8 says she tells them to go back to their mothers' homes. She is not asking them to stay with her but urging them to return. Naomi is trying to release them, not gather them in.

Baked just right. Ruth 1:9 says, "May the LORD enable each of you to find rest in the home of your new husband." Naomi is asking for a future place of rest for both women. She is blessing them even while trying to send them away.

The text really does say it. In Ruth 1:9, Naomi prays that the LORD will enable each of them to find rest in the home of a new husband. So this statement is true, not false. Naomi is picturing a settled future for them away from her.

explanations.answer: We will return with you to your people
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Ruth 1:10 says they answered Naomi, "Surely we will return with you to your people." At this point, both Orpah and Ruth say the same thing. The road gets more personal from here.

explanations.answer: We will stay in Moab and wait for you
explanations.explanation: That is not what they say. Ruth 1:10 says Orpah and Ruth tell Naomi, "Surely we will return with you to your people." They are not staying behind in Moab at this moment. Both women speak as if they are going with her.

explanations.answer: We will come visit you in Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: Not quite. Ruth 1:10 says they tell Naomi they will return with her to her people. That is stronger than talking about a visit. In this moment, both daughters-in-law are saying they want to go with Naomi herself.

explanations.answer: Would you wait for them to grow up
explanations.explanation: That is the question Naomi asks. In Ruth 1:13, she says, "Would you wait for them to grow up?" She is pressing the point that there is no practical future for them by staying with her. Naomi is talking straight, and it lands hard.

explanations.answer: Would you raise them as your own
explanations.explanation: Naomi does not ask that. In Ruth 1:13, her question is, "Would you wait for them to grow up?" She is speaking about the long wait that would be required if she somehow had sons. Her point is that this is not a path for Orpah and Ruth.

explanations.answer: Would you go ahead to Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: That is not Naomi's question in the verse. Ruth 1:13 says she asks, "Would you wait for them to grow up?" Naomi is not arranging travel plans here. She is showing why she thinks her daughters-in-law should return home.

explanations.answer: The LORD's hand has turned against her
explanations.explanation: Yes. Ruth 1:13 says Naomi believes it is more bitter for her because "the hand of the LORD has gone out against me." That is how Naomi speaks about her suffering in this moment. The verse lets you hear her pain in her own words.

explanations.answer: The people of Judah have turned against her
explanations.explanation: The text does not say that. Ruth 1:13 gives Naomi's reason as this: "the hand of the LORD has gone out against me." She does not blame the people of Judah here. She speaks about what she believes the LORD has done.

explanations.answer: The people of Moab have turned against her
explanations.explanation: That is not Naomi's explanation in the verse. Ruth 1:13 says, "the hand of the LORD has gone out against me." The passage does not say the people of Moab turned against her. Naomi's words point in a different direction.
That is true. Ruth 1:14 says, "Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clung to her." So Orpah does part from Naomi at this point. One kiss goodbye, and the two roads separate.

The verse says the opposite. Ruth 1:14 says Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye. So this statement is true, not false. The contrast in the verse is between Orpah's goodbye and Ruth clinging to Naomi.
This one came out burnt, friend. Ruth 1:14 says Orpah kissed Naomi goodbye, but Ruth clung to her. So Ruth does not go back home with Orpah. The text draws that line very clearly.
That is right. Ruth 1:14 says Ruth clung to Naomi, which means she did not go back home with Orpah. One daughter-in-law leaves, and the other stays close. That little line turns the whole story.

Yes, that is what Naomi says. Ruth 1:15 has Naomi tell Ruth, "your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and her gods; follow her back home." Naomi is still urging Ruth to leave. She has not stopped trying yet.

The verse really does say it. In Ruth 1:15, Naomi tells Ruth that Orpah has gone back to her people and her gods, and then says, "follow her back home." So this statement is true, not false. Naomi keeps pressing Ruth to return.

explanations.answer: Naomi's God will be her God
explanations.explanation: Fine work, baker! Ruth 1:16 says, "your people will be my people, and your God will be my God." Ruth is not only promising to stay with Naomi. She is also speaking about Naomi's God in a deeply personal way.

explanations.answer: She will take care of Naomi's house
explanations.explanation: Ruth promises something stronger and clearer than that. In Ruth 1:16, she says, "your people will be my people, and your God will be my God." The verse does not talk about Naomi's house. It talks about shared people and shared God.

explanations.answer: She will learn all the ways of Judah
explanations.explanation: That may fit the journey ahead, but it is not what Ruth says here. Ruth 1:16 records her words as, "your people will be my people, and your God will be my God." The promise is about belonging and loyalty. Ruth plants both feet in that sentence.

Box-worthy! Ruth 1:17 says, "May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me." Ruth is making a solemn promise. She is saying only death will part her from Naomi.

Not distance, friend. Ruth 1:17 says Ruth calls down punishment on herself if anything but death separates her and Naomi. That makes her promise weighty and final. She is not talking about miles on a road but about lifelong loyalty.

That is not the word in the verse. Ruth 1:17 says, "if anything but death separates you and me." Ruth names death as the only thing that will divide them. That is a strong promise, and she means every word of it.

explanations.answer: She stops trying to persuade her
explanations.explanation: That is right. Ruth 1:18 says when Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped trying to persuade her. Naomi sees Ruth's resolve and lets the matter rest. Ruth has said it plain enough that no more pushing will move her.

explanations.answer: She sends her back after Orpah
explanations.explanation: Naomi does not do that next. Ruth 1:18 says that when she saw Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped trying to persuade her. The argument ends there. Naomi finally sees this woman is not turning around.

explanations.answer: She tells her to wait in Moab
explanations.explanation: That is not what the verse says. Ruth 1:18 says Naomi stopped trying to persuade Ruth once she saw Ruth was determined to go with her. So there is no new instruction to wait in Moab. The talking stops, and the journey continues.

Yes indeed. Ruth 1:19 says the women of the town exclaimed, "Can this be Naomi?" Bethlehem is stirred by her return. Years have passed, and her homecoming hits the town like a door swinging open after a long silence.
That is not what the women say. Ruth 1:19 records their words as, "Can this be Naomi?" The town's first response is recognition and surprise. The verse keeps their exclamation short and pointed.

Close to the mood, but not the words. Ruth 1:19 says the women exclaim, "Can this be Naomi?" They are not treating her like a total stranger. They are startled that the woman before them is Naomi herself.

That is correct. Ruth 1:20 says, "Do not call me Naomi... Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me." Naomi gives the new name herself. The name change matches the sorrow she feels.
Not Hannah, baker. Ruth 1:20 says Naomi tells the women, "Call me Mara." She explains that request by saying the Almighty has dealt bitterly with her. So Mara is the name to remember here.

That is not the name Naomi chooses. Ruth 1:20 says she tells the women of Bethlehem, "Call me Mara." She ties that name to bitterness in her life. Leah belongs to another Bible story, but not this scene.

Still doughy, friend. Naomi says the opposite in Ruth 1:21: "I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty." So this statement is false, not true. Her words are full of loss, not satisfaction.

That is right. Ruth 1:21 says, "I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty." The statement in the question flips Naomi's words around, so it is false. Naomi sees her return through grief.

Perfect bake! Ruth 1:22 says Naomi and Ruth arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest. That little note matters. The chapter began with famine in Ruth 1:1, and it ends with harvest beginning.

Not wheat in this verse. Ruth 1:22 says they arrived at the beginning of the barley harvest. The timing is part of the hope peeking into the story. After all that bitterness, the chapter closes with fields starting to fill.

That is not the harvest named here. Ruth 1:22 says Naomi and Ruth came to Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest. The writer ends the chapter with grain coming in, not olives. You can feel the story shift, just a little.
